stimulus.text:
| Society | Environment | Main way of getting food | Settlement |
| Pueblo peoples | Arid Southwest | Dry farming of maize, beans, and squash | Permanent adobe villages |
| Iroquois villagers | Northeast woodlands | Three sisters farming, with hunting and fishing | Permanent villages |
| Chinook peoples | Rainy Pacific coast | Fishing, hunting, and foraging | Permanent villages with marked social ranks |
| Great Plains peoples | Grasslands | Bison hunting on foot, with some farming in river valleys | Mobile camps for much of the year |
| Great Basin peoples | Arid basin between mountain ranges | Hunting and gathering, moving with the seasons | Mobile camps |
stimulus.source_note: Table compiled from the grounding books; see grounding.

source: original; fresh authoring; Chinook evidence from Barron's ch3 and 5 Steps ch6
stem: The Chinook of the Pacific Northwest lived in settled villages with marked social ranks, though they farmed little. What does this example best show?

options.text: Only farming peoples ever built settled villages anywhere in the Americas.
options.misconception: Ignores settled fishing villages like those of the Chinook.

options.text: Settled, ranked societies could grow from fishing and foraging, not just farming.
Pacific Northwest peoples lived as nomads because they had no farms.
Chinook villages prove that all Native societies shared one social system.
options.misconception: Stretches one society's ranks into a claim about all societies.

rationales.A: Chinook fishing villages were settled, so farming was not the only road to settled life.
rationales.B: Rich fishing and foraging supported settled villages with marked ranks, so farming was not required.
rationales.C: Chinook peoples lived in settled communities on the Columbia River, not as nomads.
rationales.D: One society's social ranks prove nothing about all Native societies sharing one system.
rationales.general:
1. Name the case. Chinook peoples lived in settled villages with marked social ranks.
2. Name their food. They fished, hunted, and foraged along the Columbia River.
3. Ask what is missing. They farmed little, yet they lived settled and ranked lives.
4. Draw the lesson. Farming is one road to settled, ranked life, and rich fishing is another.
Remember: one counterexample breaks an always claim, so keep the exception in mind.
